title.raw: Strength Training for Cyclists: Does It Really Make You Faster?
title.rendered: Strength Training for Cyclists: Does It Really Make You Faster?

content.raw:
1. What the research found

The best studies on this come from a group of Norwegian researchers. They took well-trained cyclists, kept their normal bike training, and added two gym sessions a week for one group only. After about three months:

  • The gym group were faster over 40 minutes. The riders who only cycled showed no clear improvement.
  • They were stronger at the end of long rides. After three hours of riding, the gym group could still push about 30 W more in a 5-minute all-out effort (from 371 W to 400 W on average). The bike-only group didn't improve at all.
  • It works for women too. A later study in female cyclists found the same kind of improvement.

A separate study gave cyclists just one exercise, heavy half squats, three times a week for eight weeks. They became about 5% more efficient on the bike, meaning they used less energy at the same power, and they lasted noticeably longer at a hard, steady effort.

2. Why it works

Strength training doesn't make your engine bigger. In these studies the gym didn't raise VO₂max any more than riding alone did. What changed is how well the riders used their engine:

You waste less energy. Stronger legs produce the same power at a lower cost. Over a three-hour ride, small savings add up.

You fade less. This is the part I like most for amateur riders. The biggest difference showed up at the end of a long ride, exactly when sportives and races are decided. Lower heart rate and less fatigue late in the ride is what we call durability.

It lifts the efforts that matter. A hard 40-minute effort sits close to your Critical Power. Improving it is exactly what we want from winter training. The gym groups also gained sprint power, which matters if your racing is decided in short, punchy efforts (my sprint guide covers the bike side).

3. Will it make me heavier?

This is the most common worry, especially from climbers. In these studies, the riders' thigh muscles grew but their body weight didn't change. Done alongside normal bike training, that's what usually happens. If your weight creeps up in winter, look at food and total training before blaming the gym.

4. A bonus: your bones

Cycling is brilliant for your heart but does very little for your bones, because the bike carries your weight. A large review found that road cyclists often have lower bone density than you'd expect for such fit people. Strength work and some impact (a bit of running, jumping or hiking) are a sensible addition, especially for masters riders. If you already know you have a bone-density issue, check with your doctor first.

5. How I fit strength into the winter

Winter is the most important time of the year to build the foundations, and strength is part of that. For my athletes it works on two fronts.

In the gym. Strength work is planned across the year. After the off-season transition, riders start with one lap of the winter circuit in the first month and build to two laps in months two and three. When the season starts, it drops back to one lap of a shorter in-season circuit. It usually goes on an easy day, often after a recovery ride, so it never gets in the way of the key bike sessions.

On the bike. I come from the Italian school of strength-endurance, so a lot of the strength work happens on the bike: SFR (slow, low-cadence climbing repeats at around 40–55 rpm) and strength on the flat at 60–70 rpm. These build through the winter, for example from 3×2' to 4×2' SFR, then pyramids, and always finish with some easy tempo to transfer the work.

How heavy? The studies used genuinely heavy weights, and so does my circuit where it matters most. On the leg press and leg extension, riders go from 5 reps at 90% of their max, to 10 at 80%, to 15 at 50%, then straight onto the bike to spin at 110 rpm and turn that strength into pedalling. Most other exercises are around 70% of max for 10 reps. You don't start there: pick your weights properly, learn the movements first and don't overdo it. If you've never lifted before, get someone qualified to check your technique.

No gym? No problem. If you don't have access to a gym, my athletes follow my Core & Strength Circuit at home. It uses your own body weight: squats and jump squats, single-leg squats down to a bench, jumps onto a step, push-ups, planks and side planks, and single-leg hip raises. All you need is a mat and a sturdy bench or step. It won't load your legs as heavily as the leg press, so the on-bike strength work matters even more, but it still builds strength, stability and some useful impact for your bones.

Measure it. A CP test at the start of winter and another a few months later tells us whether the gym work is showing up on the bike.

6. A few rules so it helps rather than hurts

  • Keep the gym away from your key interval days. No heavy leg session the day before a quality session, and never the night before a race.
  • Expect heavy legs for the first two or three weeks. Ease off the intensity, not the consistency.
  • The gym doesn't replace riding. In every study, the cyclists kept their normal bike training, and the long weekend ride stays the anchor of the week.
  • Don't stop completely in the season. In a follow-up study, riders who kept just one gym session a week during the racing season held on to their gains and kept improving. That's what I do with my athletes: less in season, but not zero.

7. Keep expectations realistic

These studies were small and lasted a few months, and the riders were already well trained. Your results will depend on you, your starting point and how well the work fits around the rest of your life. There's no magic formula. Consistency over months beats one perfect week.

Final thoughts

If you want to be stronger in the last hour of a ride, not just the first, strength work is one of the best-supported things you can add to your winter. Build it up sensibly, keep a little of it in season, and plan it around your riding.

The hard part is fitting it into your week without compromising the training that matters most. That is exactly what we plan together in coaching. If you'd like a winter programme that combines strength work, CP testing and structured riding, have a look at my individual coaching packages or get in touch.

Further reading

  • Rønnestad, Hansen & Raastad (2011), Strength training improves 5-min all-out performance following 185 min of cycling. Link
  • Rønnestad, Hansen & Raastad (2010), Effect of heavy strength training on thigh muscle cross-sectional area, performance determinants, and performance in well-trained cyclists. Link
  • Sunde et al. (2010), Maximal strength training improves cycling economy in competitive cyclists. Link
  • Olmedillas et al. (2012), Cycling and bone health: a systematic review. Link

Matteo Cigala
Founder & Head Coach

excerpt.raw:
Every winter the same question comes up: should I be in the gym, or is that time better spent on the bike?

The short answer is yes, strength work makes cyclists faster, and it doesn't have to make you heavier. But it only works if it's planned around your riding, not piled on top of it. Here is what the research found, in plain terms, and how I fit it into a rider's winter.

title.raw: Slower in Winter? It's Not Your Legs
title.rendered: Slower in Winter? It’s Not Your Legs

content.raw:
Winter slows you down through three separate mechanisms that stack. Understanding them is the
difference between a rider who panics in December and one who arrives in spring fresh and fast.

The short version, with real numbers

Here is a simple model of one rider on a flat road with no wind, holding a steady 200 W. The only thing
that changes is the temperature. Rider and bike weigh 72 kg, CdA is 0.36 m² (hands on the hoods), Crr is
0.0045, drivetrain efficiency is 97.5%, at sea level in dry air.

Between 25°C and 5°C the air is 7.2% denser. To hold 32 km/h you need about 182 W in summer and
about 194 W at 5°C, which is 11 W more for the same speed. At 40 km/h the gap grows to about 22 W
(336 W vs 358 W), because the power needed to beat the air rises with the cube of speed.

Now add what winter really looks like: a jacket, thermal tights and overshoes. If I add just 0.02 m² to CdA
and 10% to Crr, the same 200 W at 5°C gives 31.7 km/h and a 60 km time of 1:53:39. That is nearly 5
minutes slower than summer on the same legs. To hold 32 km/h in that kit you need about 206 W, 23
W more than in July.

The physics in one line

The power you must produce on the flat is the sum of air resistance, rolling resistance, and the small loss
in your drivetrain:

P = \frac{\tfrac{1}{2}\,\rho\,C_dA\,v^3 + C_{rr}\,m\,g\,v}{\eta}

Here ρ is air density, CdA is your drag area, v is speed, Crr is the rolling resistance coefficient, m is rider
plus bike mass, g is 9.81 m/s² and η is drivetrain efficiency. Cold changes two of these terms directly (ρ
goes up, Crr goes up), and winter clothing changes a third (CdA).

At 32 km/h about 84% of the power in my model goes into the air. At 40 km/h it is 89%. At 20 km/h it
falls to 67%. So the faster you ride on the flat, the more the weather taxes you, and the less it matters
on a steep climb at low speed.

What the research says

  1. Cold air is a heavier air.
    A 2019 study in the Journal of Biomechanics (Beaumont and colleagues)
    combined computer fluid simulation with a power model across −10°C to 40°C. It found that the power
    needed to hold a constant speed drops as temperature rises, because aerodynamic resistance drops. A
    separate numerical analysis of freezing to scorching conditions put the change in total drag at roughly
    2.8% for every 10°C. That matches my table: 20°C of difference is about 5.6% in drag, and about 6% in
    power at 32 km/h once rolling resistance is included. Track cycling takes this seriously: engineers
    working on the London velodrome estimated that warming the air from 20°C to 25°C is worth roughly
    1.4 seconds over 4 km for a world-class pursuiter.

  2. Cold tyres roll worse.
    Rolling resistance is not a constant. In a lab test series,
    bicyclerollingresistance.com found that raising tyre surface temperature from 20°C to 40°C cut rolling
    resistance by 17.6% on average. Rothhämel (2023, International Journal of Vehicle Systems Modelling
    and Testing) measured the same trend with ambient temperature: as it falls, the coefficient rises,
    especially in the range above freezing. Higher pressure lowers it, which is one reason a slightly firmer
    tyre can help on a clean, dry winter road. On wet or gritty roads, grip comes first.

  3. Cold muscles make less power.
    This is the part most riders underestimate. A review by Racinais and
    Oksa (2010, Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports) reports that in short-duration exercise
    performance changes by around 2% to 5% for each 1°C of muscle temperature. Earlier work by Davies
    and Young (1983, Journal of Applied Physiology) showed that peak cycling power rises and falls in a
    straight line with muscle temperature: cooling the muscle by 8.4°C reduced force, while warming it by
    3.1°C sped up the contraction. A 2009 study by Racinais and colleagues found that pre-cooling the legs
    lowered sprint power, and their advice to athletes was simple: never cool the legs before a sprint.
    My reading as a coach: this third effect matters most in the first 20 to 30 minutes, on hard efforts and
    on sprints. Once you are warm and riding steady, the air and the tyres are doing most of the damage.
    That is why a winter ride often feels "flat" early and then settles.

Why your winter average looks worse than the model

The model above is clean. Real winter adds friction in every direction:

  • Wet roads and spray raise rolling resistance beyond what dry-road lab tests show.
  • Cold chain lubricant and stiffer bearings cost a few extra watts.
  • Gloves, buffs and thick layers raise CdA more than my 0.02 m² if they flap.
  • Stop-start riding, traffic lights and ice patches reduce your steady average.
    Add all of that up and a rider who is exactly as fit as in August can easily be 3% to 6% slower on the same
    route. That is not lost fitness. That is physics.

How I coach riders through the cold months

1- Judge fitness by power, not speed. If your watts for a given perceived effort or heart rate are
stable, your engine is stable.

2- Compare winter to winter. Use the same loop in similar temperatures, or run a fixed test
indoors where nothing else moves.

3- Warm up longer than you think. The research says muscle temperature drives power. Ten extra
minutes of easy spinning before the first hard effort is cheap insurance.

4- Dress to stay warm, not to be heavy. A close-fitting layer flaps less and costs fewer watts than a
loose, bulky one. Do not freeze to save drag, because a cold muscle costs you more than a
flapping jacket.

5- Reset your speed targets. Plan a group ride or a tour stage with a lower average speed in the
cold, and keep the effort the same.

6- Keep the base work honest. Winter is for aerobic volume and strength. Do not chase a summer
average in December and arrive in spring tired.


Honest caveats

My table is a model, not a lab test. It assumes dry air at standard pressure, no wind, steady effort, a flat
road and the same rider position. Your CdA, mass and tyres will differ, so your numbers will too. Wind,
altitude, humidity and drafting can easily outweigh any of the figures above. Use the table to
understand the direction and the rough size of the effect, and trust your own power file for the rest.

    The takeaway

    If you are slower in winter, check three things before you doubt your fitness: the air density, the tyres
    and the temperature of your legs. Then check your power. In most cases the engine is fine and the
    environment is the culprit.
    Send this to the friend who is convinced they lost their form in November.
    Want a winter plan that builds your base without chasing numbers that do not matter? Get in touch
    about coaching at staging.coaching.cigalacycling.com.

    Sources

    Engineering Sport, The heat is on for cyclists in the London velodrome

    Beaumont F. et al. (2019), Aerodynamic investigation of the thermo-dependent flow structure in
    the wake of a cyclist, Journal of Biomechanics 82:387–391. Abstract

    Racinais S., Oksa J. (2010), Temperature and neuromuscular function, Scandinavian Journal of
    Medicine & Science in Sports 20(S3):1–18. Record

    Davies C.T.M., Young K. (1983), Effect of temperature on the contractile properties and muscle
    power of triceps surae in humans, Journal of Applied Physiology 55(1):191–195. PubMed

    Racinais S. et al. (2009), Does the diurnal increase in central temperature interact with pre-
    cooling or passive warm-up of the leg?, Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. Abstract

    Rothhämel M. (2023), On rolling resistance of bicycle tyres with ambient temperature in focus,
    International Journal of Vehicle Systems Modelling and Testing. Summary

    bicyclerollingresistance.com, CRR at different temperatures

    Matteo Cigala
    Founder & Head Coach

1- Judge fitness by power, not speed. If your watts for a given perceived effort or heart rate are
stable, your engine is stable.

2- Compare winter to winter. Use the same loop in similar temperatures, or run a fixed test
indoors where nothing else moves.

3- Warm up longer than you think. The research says muscle temperature drives power. Ten extra
minutes of easy spinning before the first hard effort is cheap insurance.

4- Dress to stay warm, not to be heavy. A close-fitting layer flaps less and costs fewer watts than a
loose, bulky one. Do not freeze to save drag, because a cold muscle costs you more than a
flapping jacket.

5- Reset your speed targets. Plan a group ride or a tour stage with a lower average speed in the
cold, and keep the effort the same.

6- Keep the base work honest. Winter is for aerobic volume and strength. Do not chase a summer
average in December and arrive in spring tired.


Honest caveats

My table is a model, not a lab test. It assumes dry air at standard pressure, no wind, steady effort, a flat
road and the same rider position. Your CdA, mass and tyres will differ, so your numbers will too. Wind,
altitude, humidity and drafting can easily outweigh any of the figures above. Use the table to
understand the direction and the rough size of the effect, and trust your own power file for the rest.

    The takeaway

    If you are slower in winter, check three things before you doubt your fitness: the air density, the tyres
    and the temperature of your legs. Then check your power. In most cases the engine is fine and the
    environment is the culprit.
    Send this to the friend who is convinced they lost their form in November.
    Want a winter plan that builds your base without chasing numbers that do not matter? Get in touch
    about coaching at staging.coaching.cigalacycling.com.

    Sources

    Engineering Sport, The heat is on for cyclists in the London velodrome

    Beaumont F. et al. (2019), Aerodynamic investigation of the thermo-dependent flow structure in
    the wake of a cyclist, Journal of Biomechanics 82:387–391. Abstract

    Racinais S., Oksa J. (2010), Temperature and neuromuscular function, Scandinavian Journal of
    Medicine & Science in Sports 20(S3):1–18. Record

    Davies C.T.M., Young K. (1983), Effect of temperature on the contractile properties and muscle
    power of triceps surae in humans, Journal of Applied Physiology 55(1):191–195. PubMed

    Racinais S. et al. (2009), Does the diurnal increase in central temperature interact with pre-
    cooling or passive warm-up of the leg?, Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. Abstract

    Rothhämel M. (2023), On rolling resistance of bicycle tyres with ambient temperature in focus,
    International Journal of Vehicle Systems Modelling and Testing. Summary

    Founder & Head Coach

title.raw: Critical Power Testing: How to Get Reliable Data
title.rendered: Critical Power Testing: How to Get Reliable Data

content.raw:
A good CP test should give us a reliable estimate of your power-duration relationship, including CP and, depending on the protocol, W′ (W-prime).

The quality of the data depends heavily on how the test is performed.

1. Understand what we are actually testing

The CP model describes the relationship between the power you can sustain and the duration for which you can sustain it.

In its simplest form:

Work = CP × time + W′

Where:

  • CP represents the sustainable aerobic power associated with the asymptote of the power-duration relationship.
  • W′ represents a finite amount of work that can be performed above CP.

This is why we need maximal efforts of different durations.

A single 20-minute effort cannot properly describe your entire power-duration curve.

2. Choose appropriate test durations

For a traditional 3-point CP test, the efforts should be sufficiently separated in duration to provide useful information about the curve.

For example:

3 min + 7 min + 12 min

or

3 min + 12 min + 20 min

The exact protocol can vary, but the important principle is that the efforts should provide different physiological demands.

A very short effort is heavily influenced by anaerobic capacity and W′, while longer efforts increasingly reflect aerobic energy production and the sustainable portion of the power-duration curve.

The more appropriate the duration range, the more useful the resulting model.

3. The efforts need to be genuinely maximal

This is critical.

A CP model assumes that each trial represents a maximal effort for that duration.

If you ride a 5-minute effort at 95% of what you are capable of because you are afraid of blowing up, the resulting CP calculation can be distorted.

Equally, if you start far too hard and dramatically fade, the effort may be influenced by pacing error rather than your actual physiological capacity.

The objective is therefore:

Maximal sustainable power for the prescribed duration.

Not simply the highest power you can produce in the first 30 seconds.

4. Pacing is part of the test

Different durations require different pacing strategies.

For a short effort, you can tolerate a relatively high initial power because W′ contributes significantly to the effort.

For a longer effort, starting substantially above your sustainable level can deplete W′ too quickly and cause a large power decline.

A useful approach is to think about the effort as:

Aggressive → controlled → empty the tank

rather than:

Sprint → survive → fade

The objective is to minimise pacing error while still producing a maximal result.

5. Recovery between efforts matters

Recovery needs to be long enough to allow you to repeat a maximal effort, but the protocol should still be standardised.

The problem with insufficient recovery is obvious: the second and third efforts may become limited by residual fatigue and incomplete recovery of W′, rather than by the physiological capacity we are trying to measure.

However, excessive or inconsistent recovery can also affect the test.

Therefore, use the same recovery duration every time you repeat the protocol.

Consistency is extremely important when comparing tests.

6. Start the test in a controlled physiological state

Try to standardise:

  • Sleep
  • Nutrition
  • Hydration
  • Caffeine intake
  • Time of day
  • Training load beforehand
  • Temperature
  • Cooling
  • Bike and power meter

You don’t necessarily need perfect laboratory conditions.

You need repeatable conditions.

If your first test is performed at 8am after a rest day in 15°C and your next test is performed at 6pm after a hard training block in 30°C, changes in the result become much harder to interpret.

7. Temperature and cooling are particularly important

Indoor testing can be significantly affected by thermoregulation.

During a maximal effort, metabolic heat production is very high. If cooling is inadequate, core temperature can rise and cardiovascular strain can increase.

A strong fan isn’t just about comfort.

It can influence your ability to sustain power.

Therefore, if you test indoors, use consistent and adequate airflow every time.

8. Don’t rely on FTP alone

One of the advantages of CP testing is that it gives us more information than a single threshold number.

Two riders can have a similar CP but very different:

  • 1-minute power
  • 3-minute power
  • 5-minute power
  • W′
  • fatigue resistance
  • power-duration curves

This is why I prefer looking at the entire power-duration relationship rather than simply asking:

“What is your FTP?”

CP gives us another way of understanding the interaction between aerobic power and finite work capacity above CP.

9. Look at the data, not just the result

After the test, I want to see the complete files.

Important variables include:

Power → duration → cadence → heart rate → pacing → W′ → CP

I also want to know how the efforts felt.

For example, two tests could produce the same CP but very different physiological responses.

The combination of objective data and subjective feedback gives us much more information than a single number.

10. Don’t test too frequently

Testing itself creates a significant training stimulus.

Repeated maximal efforts have a cost, particularly when using protocols involving several maximal efforts.

The purpose of testing is therefore not to constantly chase a new number.

The purpose is to measure adaptation.

If training is working, we should eventually see changes in the power-duration relationship.

That could mean:

  • Higher CP
  • Increased power at longer durations
  • Increased W′
  • Improved durability
  • Reduced physiological cost at a given power
  • Improved ability to repeat high-intensity efforts

The interesting question isn’t simply:

“Did my CP increase?”

It’s:

“How has my entire performance profile changed?”

The most important principle

A CP test is a measurement tool.

To make it useful, we need to control as many variables as possible and ensure that the efforts genuinely represent your maximal capacity for those durations.

Good testing = good data.

And good data allows us to make better training decisions.

Matteo Cigala
Founder & Head Coach

title.raw: The Off-Season Transition: Does Every Cyclist Need One?
title.rendered: The Off-Season Transition: Does Every Cyclist Need One?

content.raw:
As the cycling season comes to an end, one of the most common questions is: how much time should I take off the bike?

My answer is simple: it depends on the individual.

There is no universal rule, no magic number of days and no off-season formula that works for every cyclist.

A rider training six or seven hours per week, with relatively low training stress and limited racing, is in a very different situation from someone training 12–15 hours per week, completing demanding intervals, racing regularly and pushing their body for months without a meaningful break.

Treating these two athletes in exactly the same way makes little sense.

The objective of the off-season transition is not simply to stop training because the calendar says the season is over. It’s to assess where you are, understand what your body needs and make the right decisions to prepare for the next training cycle.

1. Training load matters

The first thing to consider is how much work you’ve accumulated throughout the season.

How many hours do you train each week? How intense are your sessions? How many races, gran fondos and demanding events have you completed? Have you had adequate recovery between them?

Weekly training volume is important, but it doesn’t tell the whole story. Two cyclists training 12 hours per week can have very different fatigue levels depending on intensity, training history, sleep, nutrition, life stress and their individual response to training.

For someone riding six or seven hours per week at a manageable intensity, reducing training volume and removing structured intensity for a while may be sufficient.

For an athlete consistently training 10, 12 or 15 hours per week, particularly with frequent racing and demanding sessions, the need for a proper recovery period deserves much more attention.

The higher the accumulated training load, the more carefully we need to assess how much recovery is required.

This doesn’t mean every high-volume cyclist automatically needs the same number of days off. It means the decision needs to be made based on the athlete, not a generic calendar.

2. Does everyone need an off-season transition?

Not necessarily.

Some cyclists can finish their season, reduce their training load and continue riding without any need for a clearly defined break. Others may benefit from several weeks of reduced training, while some may need a period completely off the bike.

Consider a cyclist who trains six hours per week, rides mostly at a comfortable intensity, races occasionally and finishes the season feeling fresh. There may be little reason to prescribe a complete break from cycling.

Now consider an athlete who has trained 12–15 hours per week, raced almost every weekend and accumulated substantial fatigue over several months. That athlete may benefit significantly from a period of recovery.

These are very different scenarios.

The decision should take into account training history, accumulated fatigue, recent performance, motivation, physical condition and upcoming goals.

The mistake is assuming that everyone needs an off-season simply because it’s October or November.

Equally, assuming you don’t need one because you can still hit your power targets can be misleading. It’s possible to maintain good performance while carrying fatigue.

The goal isn’t to prescribe recovery unnecessarily, nor to avoid it at all costs. It’s to identify what the individual actually needs.

3. When is time completely off the bike important?

For cyclists who train consistently throughout the year, taking a period completely off the bike can be one of the most valuable parts of the transition.

But it isn’t necessary for everyone.

If your training volume is relatively low, your sessions are manageable and you’re recovering well, reducing the demands of training may be enough.

However, if you’ve spent months accumulating substantial training hours, completing demanding intervals and racing frequently, a complete break may be appropriate.

Why?

Because recovery isn’t always about making every session easier. Sometimes, it’s about temporarily removing the demands of cycling altogether.

Taking time away from the bike gives you a break from structured sessions, power targets, training metrics and the pressure to maintain fitness. It also creates an opportunity to address minor niggles, catch up on sleep, spend time with family and friends, and enjoy activities that may have taken a back seat during the season.

For some athletes, a complete break of around one to two weeks can be a reasonable starting point. Others may need less or more, depending on their circumstances.

There is no magic number.

Time off the bike should be a response to the athlete’s needs, not a rule that everyone must follow.

4. But won’t you lose fitness?

Yes, some fitness may decline when you reduce or stop training. That’s normal.

Your aerobic adaptations and performance-specific conditioning are influenced by how much training you do. A sufficiently long period of inactivity can reduce some of those adaptations.

But the important question is not whether you might lose a little fitness.

It’s whether maintaining every last watt throughout the off-season is worth sacrificing the opportunity to recover and start your next preparation block in a better position.

You don’t need to maintain peak condition for 12 months of the year.

You need to be prepared to perform when it matters.

A short, planned break is very different from abandoning training for months. The objective is to step away temporarily when appropriate, then return progressively when you’re ready.

Don’t confuse a temporary reduction in fitness with losing the progress you’ve made over years of consistent training.

Remember: your long-term development depends on the quality and consistency of your training over multiple seasons, not on whether you maintain your best numbers every week of the year.

5. Use the off-season to explore other sports and activities

The transition period can also be an excellent opportunity to step away from cycling and introduce some variety into your routine.

When you’re training consistently throughout the year, most of your physical activity revolves around riding a bike. Although cycling develops excellent aerobic fitness, it doesn’t challenge every aspect of your physical capacity.

Depending on your training history and individual needs, the off-season can be a good time to incorporate activities such as:

  • Walking and hiking.
  • Swimming.
  • Running, if you’re accustomed to it or introduce it gradually.
  • Gym-based strength training.
  • Mobility work and other general physical activities.

There are several potential benefits.

First, variety. Doing something different can help you mentally disconnect from structured cycling and return with renewed motivation.

Second, general athletic development. Strength training can improve muscular strength and address weaknesses that cycling alone may not adequately develop. Other activities can challenge different movement patterns, coordination and general fitness.

Third, a change from repetitive cycling-specific demands. After months of pedalling, a different activity can provide a welcome physical and mental change.

However, alternative sports are not automatically recovery activities. Running, for example, introduces impact forces and can cause significant muscle soreness in cyclists who aren’t accustomed to it.

And there is an important distinction: if you’re taking time off because you’ve accumulated substantial fatigue, replacing 12 hours of cycling with 12 hours of running, gym sessions and other demanding activities defeats the purpose.

The objective is not to maintain the same training load through different sports.

It’s to recover, enjoy movement and, where appropriate, develop qualities that will benefit you in the long term.

Rest should remain the priority when recovery is what you need.

6. This is where your coach becomes particularly important

The off-season transition is one of the periods when having a coach can make a real difference.

During the racing season, the focus is often on executing the training plan, preparing for events and managing performance.

At the end of the season, the question changes: what does this particular athlete need now?

A good coach should look beyond the number of hours completed and assess the bigger picture.

This includes:

Training history: Weekly volume, intensity, consistency and accumulated workload.

Racing demands: The number of events completed, their duration and intensity, and the recovery available between them.

Performance trends: Whether the athlete has continued to improve, plateaued or experienced a decline.

Recovery indicators: Sleep, perceived fatigue, motivation and the athlete’s response to training.

Life outside cycling: Work, family responsibilities, stress and other factors affecting recovery.

Next season’s objectives: When the athlete needs to be ready and how much preparation time is available.

No single metric can make this decision. Power data, training load and performance trends are useful, but they must be interpreted alongside the athlete’s feedback and wider circumstances.

The coach’s role is to bring these pieces together and decide when to reduce training, whether a complete break is appropriate, and when to begin building again.

Timing matters.

Too little recovery when fatigue is high may mean carrying that fatigue into the next training block. Conversely, prescribing an unnecessarily long break without considering the athlete’s goals may delay preparation without providing additional benefit.

The objective is to get the timing right for that individual athlete.

Good coaching isn’t just about knowing when to push. It’s also about knowing when to pull back.

7. Review your season before planning the next one

The transition period is also an opportunity to review your performance objectively.

Instead of immediately jumping into another training plan, ask yourself what the previous season has taught you.

Consider the following questions:

  • Did you perform as expected in your key events?
  • Were you strong at the start of races but faded towards the end?
  • Could you produce high power when fresh but struggle after several hours?
  • Did your performance improve throughout the season, or did you plateau?
  • Were you consistent with your training and nutrition?
  • Did you struggle to balance training with work, family and recovery?
  • Were there periods when you trained hard but saw little improvement?

Your answers should help identify the areas that deserve attention next season.

Perhaps you need better aerobic durability, improved fuelling, greater repeatability during hard efforts or a more sustainable approach to training.

Maybe the issue wasn’t fitness at all, but inconsistency or insufficient recovery.

Repeating the same training year after year without evaluating the results is not a strategy for continuous improvement.

It’s simply repetition.

8. Remember that cycling performance is more than FTP

The off-season is also a useful time to look beyond a single power number.

FTP is a valuable training reference, but it doesn’t fully describe your ability to perform over a long event.

Your critical power, W′, aerobic capacity, durability, fuelling strategy and ability to recover between efforts all contribute to performance in different ways.

For example, two cyclists with similar threshold power can have very different results in a five-hour gran fondo. One may maintain power exceptionally well after several hours, while the other experiences a significant decline as fatigue accumulates.

That difference matters.

Rather than entering the new season focused exclusively on increasing FTP, consider your broader performance profile.

Where are your strengths? Where are your limitations? What does your target event actually demand?

These answers should influence the training you prioritise when structured preparation resumes.

9. How should you return to training?

Once the appropriate recovery period has been completed, avoid jumping straight back into the same workload you were completing at the end of the season.

Start with easy, enjoyable rides and gradually rebuild consistency. Reintroduce structure and increase training demands according to your response.

For some cyclists, the transition may be as simple as reducing training volume and removing structured intensity before progressively returning to normal training.

For others, it may involve a complete break, a period of alternative activities and a more gradual return to cycling.

There is no need to force a fixed sequence or duration. Your training background, recovery and goals should determine the approach.

The objective is to begin the next training block ready to absorb the work, rather than carrying unnecessary fatigue into another season.

Final thoughts

There is no one-size-fits-all approach to the off-season.

A cyclist training six or seven hours per week is not necessarily in the same position as someone training 12–15 hours, racing frequently and accumulating substantial fatigue throughout a long season.

Some athletes will benefit from a period completely off the bike. Others may only need to reduce their training load and intensity. Some may not need a clearly defined transition at all.

The important thing is to understand the difference.

Don’t take time off simply because somebody else does. And don’t keep riding simply because you’re afraid of losing fitness.

Assess the workload, consider the fatigue, review the season and make a decision based on the individual.

Use the transition to recover when necessary, explore other activities where appropriate, and prepare intelligently for the demands of the next season.

Ultimately, the goal isn’t to finish the off-season with the highest fitness possible.

It’s to start your next season ready to train, adapt and perform.

Train smarter. Recover with purpose. Build for the long term.

Matteo Cigala
Founder & Head Coach

As the cycling season comes to an end, one of the most common questions is: how much time should I take off the bike?

My answer is simple: it depends on the individual.

There is no universal rule, no magic number of days and no off-season formula that works for every cyclist.

A rider training six or seven hours per week, with relatively low training stress and limited racing, is in a very different situation from someone training 12–15 hours per week, completing demanding intervals, racing regularly and pushing their body for months without a meaningful break.

Treating these two athletes in exactly the same way makes little sense.

The objective of the off-season transition is not simply to stop training because the calendar says the season is over. It’s to assess where you are, understand what your body needs and make the right decisions to prepare for the next training cycle.

1. Training load matters

The first thing to consider is how much work you’ve accumulated throughout the season.

How many hours do you train each week? How intense are your sessions? How many races, gran fondos and demanding events have you completed? Have you had adequate recovery between them?

Weekly training volume is important, but it doesn’t tell the whole story. Two cyclists training 12 hours per week can have very different fatigue levels depending on intensity, training history, sleep, nutrition, life stress and their individual response to training.

For someone riding six or seven hours per week at a manageable intensity, reducing training volume and removing structured intensity for a while may be sufficient.

For an athlete consistently training 10, 12 or 15 hours per week, particularly with frequent racing and demanding sessions, the need for a proper recovery period deserves much more attention.

The higher the accumulated training load, the more carefully we need to assess how much recovery is required.

This doesn’t mean every high-volume cyclist automatically needs the same number of days off. It means the decision needs to be made based on the athlete, not a generic calendar.

2. Does everyone need an off-season transition?

Not necessarily.

Some cyclists can finish their season, reduce their training load and continue riding without any need for a clearly defined break. Others may benefit from several weeks of reduced training, while some may need a period completely off the bike.

Consider a cyclist who trains six hours per week, rides mostly at a comfortable intensity, races occasionally and finishes the season feeling fresh. There may be little reason to prescribe a complete break from cycling.

Now consider an athlete who has trained 12–15 hours per week, raced almost every weekend and accumulated substantial fatigue over several months. That athlete may benefit significantly from a period of recovery.

These are very different scenarios.

The decision should take into account training history, accumulated fatigue, recent performance, motivation, physical condition and upcoming goals.

The mistake is assuming that everyone needs an off-season simply because it’s October or November.

Equally, assuming you don’t need one because you can still hit your power targets can be misleading. It’s possible to maintain good performance while carrying fatigue.

The goal isn’t to prescribe recovery unnecessarily, nor to avoid it at all costs. It’s to identify what the individual actually needs.

3. When is time completely off the bike important?

For cyclists who train consistently throughout the year, taking a period completely off the bike can be one of the most valuable parts of the transition.

But it isn’t necessary for everyone.

If your training volume is relatively low, your sessions are manageable and you’re recovering well, reducing the demands of training may be enough.

However, if you’ve spent months accumulating substantial training hours, completing demanding intervals and racing frequently, a complete break may be appropriate.

Why?

Because recovery isn’t always about making every session easier. Sometimes, it’s about temporarily removing the demands of cycling altogether.

Taking time away from the bike gives you a break from structured sessions, power targets, training metrics and the pressure to maintain fitness. It also creates an opportunity to address minor niggles, catch up on sleep, spend time with family and friends, and enjoy activities that may have taken a back seat during the season.

For some athletes, a complete break of around one to two weeks can be a reasonable starting point. Others may need less or more, depending on their circumstances.

There is no magic number.

Time off the bike should be a response to the athlete’s needs, not a rule that everyone must follow.

4. But won’t you lose fitness?

Yes, some fitness may decline when you reduce or stop training. That’s normal.

Your aerobic adaptations and performance-specific conditioning are influenced by how much training you do. A sufficiently long period of inactivity can reduce some of those adaptations.

But the important question is not whether you might lose a little fitness.

It’s whether maintaining every last watt throughout the off-season is worth sacrificing the opportunity to recover and start your next preparation block in a better position.

You don’t need to maintain peak condition for 12 months of the year.

You need to be prepared to perform when it matters.

A short, planned break is very different from abandoning training for months. The objective is to step away temporarily when appropriate, then return progressively when you’re ready.

Don’t confuse a temporary reduction in fitness with losing the progress you’ve made over years of consistent training.

Remember: your long-term development depends on the quality and consistency of your training over multiple seasons, not on whether you maintain your best numbers every week of the year.

5. Use the off-season to explore other sports and activities

The transition period can also be an excellent opportunity to step away from cycling and introduce some variety into your routine.

When you’re training consistently throughout the year, most of your physical activity revolves around riding a bike. Although cycling develops excellent aerobic fitness, it doesn’t challenge every aspect of your physical capacity.

Depending on your training history and individual needs, the off-season can be a good time to incorporate activities such as:

  • Walking and hiking.
  • Swimming.
  • Running, if you’re accustomed to it or introduce it gradually.
  • Gym-based strength training.
  • Mobility work and other general physical activities.

There are several potential benefits.

First, variety. Doing something different can help you mentally disconnect from structured cycling and return with renewed motivation.

Second, general athletic development. Strength training can improve muscular strength and address weaknesses that cycling alone may not adequately develop. Other activities can challenge different movement patterns, coordination and general fitness.

Third, a change from repetitive cycling-specific demands. After months of pedalling, a different activity can provide a welcome physical and mental change.

However, alternative sports are not automatically recovery activities. Running, for example, introduces impact forces and can cause significant muscle soreness in cyclists who aren’t accustomed to it.

And there is an important distinction: if you’re taking time off because you’ve accumulated substantial fatigue, replacing 12 hours of cycling with 12 hours of running, gym sessions and other demanding activities defeats the purpose.

The objective is not to maintain the same training load through different sports.

It’s to recover, enjoy movement and, where appropriate, develop qualities that will benefit you in the long term.

Rest should remain the priority when recovery is what you need.

The objective is to get the timing right for that individual athlete.

Good coaching isn’t just about knowing when to push. It’s also about knowing when to pull back.

title.raw: AI Cycling Coaching: Why Great Coaching Is More Than a Training Plan
title.rendered: AI Cycling Coaching: Why Great Coaching Is More Than a Training Plan

content.raw:
One thing has become incredibly clear.

The athletes who improve the most aren't necessarily the ones with the best genetics, the most expensive bike or even the most time to train.

They're the athletes making the right decisions consistently.

And that's exactly where coaching goes far beyond simply writing workouts.

The Biggest Misconception About Coaching

Many athletes believe coaching is just about receiving a training plan.

Complete today's workout.

Repeat tomorrow.

Get faster.

If only it were that simple.

The reality is that training plans—even well-designed ones—are built on assumptions.

They assume you'll sleep well.

They assume work won't become stressful.

They assume you won't get sick.

They assume you'll recover exactly as predicted.

Life rarely follows the plan.

Great coaching isn't about creating the perfect programme.

It's about making the right decisions when reality doesn't match the programme.

Data Is Powerful. Context Is Everything.

Today's endurance athletes collect more data than ever before.

Power.

Heart rate.

Heart rate variability.

Sleep.

Recovery scores.

Nutrition.

Training load.

The challenge isn't collecting more numbers.

It's understanding what they actually mean.

I've seen athletes panic because their HRV dropped for two days.

Others increase training simply because their FTP went up.

Some ignore accumulating fatigue because their Garmin says they're "ready."

None of those decisions should be made using a single metric.

Every piece of data needs context.

That's where experience still matters.er perceived exertion, and better fatigue resistance, are exactly that — reports and anecdotes from a competitive environment with every incentive to talk up a new product, not independently verified performance data.

AI Has Changed Coaching Forever

Artificial intelligence is transforming endurance coaching, and that's a good thing.

The best AI platforms don't replace coaches.

They remove repetitive tasks, analyse huge volumes of data and surface insights that would otherwise take hours to find. Modern platforms can continuously update training zones, estimate physiological changes and personalise recommendations as new information arrives.

Instead of spending time manually updating thresholds or reviewing every training file line by line, coaches can focus on what humans do best:

  • understanding the athlete
  • making strategic decisions
  • providing motivation
  • communicating effectively
  • solving problems

That's exactly how I use Vekta.

It doesn't replace my coaching.

It amplifies it.

Coaching the Athlete, Not the Numbers

One lesson I've learned is that identical data can tell completely different stories.

Two athletes complete the same interval session.

Same power.

Same heart rate.

Same duration.

One finishes feeling confident and motivated.

The other barely survives the workout because work has been stressful for weeks and sleep has been poor.

If you only look at the numbers, both sessions appear identical.

They aren't.

Performance isn't just physiology.

It's psychology.

Lifestyle.

Nutrition.

Recovery.

Confidence.

Consistency.

The best coaching combines objective data with subjective feedback to understand the complete athlete, not just today's workout.

Why Personalisation Matters

Every athlete adapts differently.

Some thrive with high volume.

Others respond better to intensity.

Some recover quickly.

Others need more rest than the textbook suggests.

That's why generic plans can only take you so far.

Modern coaching should evolve continuously.

Training intensity should adapt.

Recovery should influence decisions.

Nutrition should match training demands.

Goals should evolve as fitness changes.

Personalisation isn't a luxury anymore.

It's becoming the expectation.als.

The Future Isn't AI vs Coaches

People often ask whether AI will replace coaches.

I don't think that's the right question.

The future isn't AI versus coaches.

It's AI helping coaches become better.

Technology gives us faster analysis.

Better insights.

Greater scalability.

Human coaches still provide judgment, empathy, accountability and trust—qualities that athletes consistently value alongside technical expertise.

That's a partnership no algorithm can replace.

Final Thoughts

The goal has never been to create the perfect training plan.

The goal is helping athletes make better decisions every single day.

Technology makes that easier.

Experience makes it meaningful.

When the two work together, athletes don't just train harder.

They train smarter.

And in endurance sport, that's often the difference between finishing with regret and reaching your biggest goals.

Matteo Cigala
Founder & Head Coach

title.raw: Come Prepararsi alla Gran Fondo Strade Bianche: La Guida di un Coach
title.rendered: Come Prepararsi alla Gran Fondo Strade Bianche: La Guida di un Coach

content.raw:
La Gran Fondo Strade Bianche è una delle manifestazioni ciclistiche più iconiche d'Italia. Partendo e arrivando a Siena, il percorso attraversa le leggendarie strade bianche della Toscana, alternando asfalto e sterrato tra continui saliscendi, muri ripidi e settori che mettono alla prova tecnica, resistenza e capacità di gestione dello sforzo.

Ho avuto il privilegio di partecipare alla Gran Fondo Strade Bianche in cinque occasioni, conquistando due vittorie sul percorso medio. Grazie a questa esperienza diretta conosco perfettamente le caratteristiche del percorso, le difficoltà dei settori sterrati e gli errori che più frequentemente compromettono la prestazione degli amatori.

Molti affrontano questa granfondo pensando che sia una normale gara su strada con qualche tratto di sterrato. In realtà è una sfida completamente diversa. Non basta avere una buona FTP o saper affrontare lunghe salite: serve essere efficienti su terreni variabili, gestire continui cambi di ritmo e arrivare agli ultimi settori con ancora energie a disposizione.

Negli ultimi anni ho preparato numerosi atleti per la Gran Fondo Strade Bianche e l'errore più comune è sempre lo stesso: allenarsi esclusivamente su strada. Il risultato? Ottima forma fisica, ma poca capacità di adattarsi alle continue richieste dello sterrato.

Perché la Gran Fondo Strade Bianche Richiede una Preparazione Diversa

A differenza di molte granfondo alpine, qui il problema non sono le lunghe salite, ma la continua alternanza tra:

  • Settori sterrati veloci e sconnessi.
  • Rampe brevi ma molto ripide.
  • Continui rilanci in uscita dalle curve.
  • Vibrazioni che aumentano la fatica muscolare.

Questo significa che dovrai sviluppare:

  • Grande capacità aerobica, per sostenere diverse ore di gara.
  • Resistenza agli sforzi ripetuti, perché i cambi di ritmo sono continui.
  • Buona tecnica di guida sullo sterrato, fondamentale per risparmiare energie.
  • Durability, ovvero la capacità di mantenere la prestazione anche dopo molte ore di gara.

Costruire la Base: 12-16 Settimane Prima

La preparazione dovrebbe iniziare con una solida base aerobica.

Ogni settimana cerca di includere:

  • Un'uscita lunga prevalentemente in Zona 2.
  • Un allenamento Sweet Spot o a soglia.
  • Una seduta dedicata alla forza resistente a bassa cadenza.
  • Se possibile, un'uscita su sterrato.

Anche pochi chilometri di gravel ogni settimana migliorano notevolmente la sicurezza e l'efficienza.

Fase Specifica: 6-8 Settimane Prima

La preparazione diventa molto più specifica.

Inserisci:

  • Lunghi con numerosi cambi di ritmo.
  • Ripetute in salita di 3-8 minuti.
  • Intervalli Over/Under.
  • Uscite gravel con discese tecniche.
  • Allenamenti dove affronti gli ultimi sforzi importanti dopo diverse ore di pedalata.

L'obiettivo non è solamente aumentare la potenza, ma imparare a produrre watt quando sei già affaticato.

Tecnica di Guida

La tecnica conta quasi quanto la condizione fisica.

Allenati a:

  • mantenere una presa rilassata sul manubrio;
  • scegliere la traiettoria migliore;
  • frenare prima della curva e non durante;
  • rilanciare rapidamente in uscita;
  • affrontare lo sterrato con fluidità invece di combatterlo.

Ogni errore tecnico costa energia preziosa.

Alimentazione

La Gran Fondo Strade Bianche è estremamente impegnativa dal punto di vista energetico.

L'obiettivo dovrebbe essere assumere:

  • 60-90 g di carboidrati all'ora
  • Idratazione costante
  • Elettroliti nelle giornate più calde

Inizia ad alimentarti già nella prima ora di gara.

Tapering: Le Ultime 2 Settimane

Riduci il volume mantenendo qualche breve richiamo ad alta intensità.

Nell'ultima settimana cura soprattutto recupero, sonno e alimentazione.

Non introdurre nuovi materiali o nuove strategie nutrizionali pochi giorni prima della gara.

Il Giorno della Gara

Le Strade Bianche premiano chi mantiene la calma.

  • Non partire troppo forte nei primi settori.
  • Evita accelerazioni inutili.
  • Mantieni una cadenza regolare sulle rampe.
  • Alimentati con regolarità.
  • Guida in maniera fluida sullo sterrato.

Molti perdono minuti preziosi semplicemente sprecando troppe energie nella prima metà della gara.

Come Prepariamo i Nostri Atleti

Ogni atleta affronta la Gran Fondo Strade Bianche con caratteristiche differenti. Alcuni arrivano dalla strada e devono migliorare la guida sullo sterrato, altri hanno esperienza gravel ma devono sviluppare maggiore resistenza sulle lunghe distanze.

Per questo motivo non utilizziamo programmi standard. Ogni piano di allenamento viene costruito in base ai tuoi obiettivi, al tempo disponibile e al tuo livello di preparazione, utilizzando metriche avanzate come Critical Power (CP), modellazione del W′ e analisi della Durability.

Che il tuo obiettivo sia completare la Gran Fondo Strade Bianche, migliorare il tuo tempo o preparare un'altra granfondo, realizziamo un percorso completamente personalizzato.

Scopri i nostri pacchetti Basic, Advanced e Premium e scegli il livello di supporto più adatto alle tue esigenze.

Scopri i nostri pacchetti di coaching a questo LINK

Vivi la Gran Fondo Strade Bianche con Cigala Cycling Tours

Ogni marzo organizziamo il nostro esclusivo Strade Bianche Cycling Tour, un'esperienza pensata per prepararti al meglio all'evento vivendo alcuni dei settori sterrati più iconici della Toscana.

Durante il tour pedalerai sulle stesse strade della granfondo, riceverai consigli tecnici direttamente da me su guida, posizionamento, ritmo e alimentazione, e potrai affrontare la gara con una conoscenza approfondita del percorso.

Il giorno prima della Gran Fondo vedremo al gara dei professionisti insieme, mentre la domenica e' il nostro turno.
Sarai supportato da noi, prima, durante e dopo la gara. Il nostro team ti fara' assistenza, passera' la borraccia come un vero pro, e sara' pronto a tutte le tue domande.

Essendo inoltre Tour Operator, inoltre con noi avrai il pettorale garantito.

Che il tuo obiettivo sia completare la tua prima Gran Fondo Strade Bianche o migliorare il tuo risultato personale, il nostro tour rappresenta il modo ideale per arrivare preparato al giorno della gara.

A questo link, troverai tutti i dettagli del nostro Strade Bianche Cycling Tour:

FAQ

Meglio bici da strada o gravel?

Per la maggior parte dei partecipanti una bici da strada con pneumatici da 30-32 mm rappresenta la soluzione migliore. Chi punta soprattutto al divertimento può valutare una bici gravel.

Quanto sterrato c'è?

Il percorso include numerosi settori di strada bianca che rappresentano una parte significativa della gara e rendono l'evento unico rispetto alle classiche granfondo.

Quanto tempo serve per prepararsi?

Se hai già una buona base aerobica, 12-16 settimane sono generalmente sufficienti. Se parti da zero, è preferibile programmare almeno 20 settimane.

Serve allenarsi sullo sterrato?

Assolutamente sì. Anche una sola uscita gravel o su strade bianche alla settimana migliora tecnica, sicurezza e gestione dello sforzo, aspetti fondamentali per affrontare al meglio la Gran Fondo Strade Bianche.

Matteo Cigala
Founder & Head Coach

title.raw: Come Allenarsi per la Maratona dles Dolomites: la Guida di un Coach
title.rendered: Come Allenarsi per la Maratona dles Dolomites: la Guida di un Coach

content.raw:
La Maratona dles Dolomites non ha bisogno di presentazioni per chi pedala in Italia. Con oltre 4.000 metri di dislivello distribuiti su percorsi che toccano i passi più iconici delle Dolomiti — Pordoi, Sella, Gardena, Campolongo, Falzarego, Giau nel percorso lungo — è una delle granfondo più desiderate al mondo, con una lista d'attesa che ogni anno supera di gran lunga i posti disponibili. Chi riesce ad accedervi, spesso dopo anni di tentativi, vuole arrivare al via nella miglior condizione possibile.

Ho seguito diversi atleti nella preparazione a questo evento, e il pattern è sempre lo stesso: chi si allena solo per il chilometraggio arriva stanco già al secondo passo, chi si allena per la specificità della salita alpina arriva forte fino a Giau. Questa guida è costruita attorno a questa differenza.

Le salite delle Dolomiti hanno una caratteristica che le distingue da molte altre granfondo italiane: pendenze relativamente costanti su lunghe distanze, spesso tra il 7% e il 9% per 10-15 km consecutivi, ad alta quota. Non sono le rampe brevi e esplosive di una classica del Nord Europa — è resistenza muscolare pura, sostenuta per 40-60 minuti alla volta, più volte in giornata.

Le tre cose che determinano davvero come arriverai all'ultimo passo:

  1. Potenza sostenibile per lungo tempo (soglia e sotto-soglia) — la capacità di mantenere un ritmo costante e efficiente per decine di minuti, non i picchi brevi.
  2. Gestione della quota — molte delle salite superano i 2000 metri, e chi non ha mai affrontato sforzi prolungati ad altitudini simili spesso sottovaluta l'impatto sulla performance.
  3. Ripetibilità su salite multiple — non si scala un solo passo, ma quattro o cinque, a distanza di ore l'uno dall'altro, con discese tecniche che affaticano braccia e concentrazione tanto quanto le gambe.

Costruire la Base: 14-18 Settimane Prima

  • Uscita lunga settimanale con salite ripetute. Se hai accesso a una salita lunga vicino a casa, usala come riferimento: l'obiettivo è mantenere un ritmo costante anche alla terza o quarta ripetizione, quando la fatica inizia a farsi sentire.
  • Lavoro specifico a soglia. Una sessione settimanale di 3-4 x 10-15 minuti a soglia (Zona 4), preferibilmente in salita, per costruire esattamente il tipo di sforzo che affronterai sui passi dolomitici.
  • Volume aerobico di base (Zona 2). Fondamentale per una giornata che spesso supera le 7-8 ore in sella — è quello che ti permette di arrivare al Giau con ancora qualcosa da dare, invece di gestire solo la sopravvivenza.

Fase Specifica: 6-8 Settimane Prima

  • Simulazioni di salite multiple in giornata, per abituare il corpo alla fatica accumulata che si prova salendo il quarto o quinto passo, non solo il primo a gambe fresche.
  • Allenamento in quota, se possibile. Anche solo qualche uscita in montagna prima dell'evento aiuta l'adattamento fisiologico e la gestione mentale della fatica ad alta quota.
  • Pratica in discesa su strade tecniche. Le discese dolomitiche, specialmente dal Giau e dal Falzarego, richiedono controllo e concentrazione — recuperare energia mentale in discesa è una skill allenabile quanto la salita stessa.

Tapering: Ultime 2 Settimane

Riduci il volume ma mantieni un minimo di intensità con brevi sforzi a soglia per rimanere reattivo. Dai priorità al sonno e alla disponibilità di carboidrati nell'ultima settimana — a questo punto il lavoro di fondo è già fatto, e l'obiettivo è arrivare al via fresco, non aggiungere altro carico.

Il Giorno della Gara: Cosa Fa Davvero la Differenza

  • Gestisci il ritmo sul Pordoi, la prima grande salita del percorso. Partire troppo forte qui è l'errore più comune, e si paga caro su Sella e Gardena più avanti.
  • Alimentati prima di avere fame, bevi prima di avere sete. Con dislivelli di questa entità, un deficit energetico accumulato nelle prime ore è molto difficile da recuperare.
  • Scegli il rapporto giusto. Una guarnitura compatta con un pacco pignoni ampio (32-34 denti) non è un vezzo su pendenze sostenute come queste — è la differenza tra gestire la cadenza e distruggere le ginocchia.

Come Costruiamo Questo in un Piano di Coaching

Chi riesce ad accedervi, spesso dopo anni di tentativi, vuole arrivare al via nella miglior condizione possibile.

Ho seguito diversi atleti nella preparazione a questo evento, e il pattern è sempre lo stesso: chi si allena solo per il chilometraggio arriva stanco già al secondo passo, chi si allena per la specificità della salita alpina arriva forte fino a Giau. Le salite delle Dolomiti hanno una caratteristica che le distingue da molte altre granfondo italiane: pendenze relativamente costanti su lunghe distanze, spesso tra il 7% e il 9% per 10-15 km consecutivi, ad alta quota.   • Uscita lunga settimanale con salite ripetute. Se hai accesso a una salita lunga vicino a casa, usala come riferimento: l’obiettivo è mantenere un ritmo costante anche alla terza o quarta ripetizione, quando la fatica inizia a farsi sentire.

title.raw: How to Train for Gran Fondo Whistler: A Coach's Guide to BC's Signature Climbing Day
title.rendered: How to Train for Gran Fondo Whistler: A Coach’s Guide to BC’s Signature Climbing Day

content.raw:
Gran Fondo Whistler has become one of the marquee events on the Canadian calendar, and the route explains why. Starting in Vancouver and finishing 122km later in Whistler Village, the ride climbs steadily through the Sea-to-Sky corridor before the defining test of the day: the Callaghan Valley climb, a sustained ascent that comes when riders are already several hours and multiple rolling climbs into the route. It's not the longest fondo in North America, but the combination of cumulative elevation gain and a hard climb positioned late in the ride catches a lot of riders out.

I've coached Canadian riders through Whistler for several seasons, and the pattern is consistent: riders who train for one big effort struggle, and riders who train for sustained, repeated climbing effort thrive. This guide is built around that distinction.

Why Whistler Is a Pacing Problem as Much as a Fitness Problem

The Sea-to-Sky Highway isn't a single brutal climb — it's a long series of rolling terrain and shorter climbs that gradually wear riders down before Callaghan Valley arrives. That structure changes what actually needs to be trained:

  • Pacing discipline in a large field. With a big, competitive start list, it's easy to get pulled into faster groups early on the Sea-to-Sky rollers — which is exactly the mistake that leaves nothing in reserve for Callaghan.
  • Sustained sub-threshold power over hours, not minutes. The rolling terrain before Callaghan rewards riders who can hold a steady, efficient effort for long stretches rather than those who rely on short bursts of power.
  • The ability to produce a hard, sustained effort on tired legs. Callaghan Valley is the true test of the day, and it comes after 90+ km of rolling terrain — riders who arrive there already depleted lose far more time than the climb's gradient alone would suggest.

Building the Engine: 12-16 Weeks Out

  • Weekly long ride with a hard effort built into the back half. Rather than front-loading intensity, structure your long ride so the hardest climbing comes after 2-3 hours in the saddle — this directly mirrors the demand of reaching Callaghan already fatigued.
  • Tempo and sub-threshold intervals. Longer efforts (15-30 minutes at 76-88% FTP) build the sustained-power capacity that the rolling Sea-to-Sky terrain specifically rewards, more so than short, sharp VO2 work.
  • Aerobic base volume. With over 2,000m of cumulative elevation across the full route, a strong aerobic engine is what determines whether Callaghan feels hard or feels impossible.

Race-Specific Phase: 6-8 Weeks Out

  • Simulate the late-race climb. On a long ride, save your hardest local climb for the final third rather than riding it fresh — this is the single most specific thing you can do to prepare for how Callaghan Valley will actually feel on race day.
  • Practice pacing in a group setting, ideally in a fast group ride or local race, to build the discipline to hold back on early rollers even when others are pushing the pace.
  • Back-to-back moderate-long rides on a weekend, to build the resilience needed for a full training block leading into a demanding one-day event.

Taper: The Final Two Weeks

Cut volume, keep a small amount of race-pace intensity to stay sharp, and prioritise sleep and carbohydrate availability in the final week. The elevation gain on this course rewards riders who arrive rested far more than riders who squeeze in one more hard week.

Race Day: What Actually Wins or Loses You the Ride

  • Resist the urge to follow fast groups through the early rollers. The Sea-to-Sky corridor is deceptively costly if ridden too hard early — the real test is still 90km away.
  • Fuel consistently through the rolling terrain, not just on the Callaghan climb itself. Energy deficits built up over the first three hours are what actually cause riders to fade on the final ascent.
  • Know the Callaghan climb before race day if you can. Even a single training visit to the Sea-to-Sky corridor removes a lot of the uncertainty that causes riders to misjudge their effort on the day.

How We Build This Into a Coaching Plan

Whistler rewards riders who can pace a long, rolling day and still produce a strong, sustained effort at the end of it — and that balance looks different depending on your current aerobic base and time-crunched training reality. As part of our cycling coaching in Canada, we build event-specific plans around your current numbers (CP, W′, FTP) and your available training time, so your preparation is built around what Callaghan Valley actually demands — not a generic fondo template.

FAQ

How much climbing is there on the Gran Fondo Whistler route? The full route from Vancouver to Whistler includes over 2,000m of cumulative elevation gain, with the Callaghan Valley climb as the decisive effort late in the ride, after a long stretch of rolling Sea-to-Sky terrain.

Is Gran Fondo Whistler a good first fondo, or is it better suited to experienced riders? It's manageable for a well-prepared newer rider, but the length and the late positioning of the hardest climb reward proper pacing discipline more than raw fitness alone — riders new to fondos benefit significantly from structured pacing practice beforehand.

What's the biggest mistake riders make on this course? Going too hard on the early rolling sections into fast groups, then arriving at Callaghan Valley with far less in reserve than they expected. Pacing discipline matters as much as fitness on this route.

How long before race day should specific preparation start? 12-16 weeks gives enough time to build both the aerobic base and the late-ride climbing strength this course demands, assuming a reasonable existing fitness level. Riders starting from a lower base should allow longer.

Matteo Cigala
Founder & Head Coach

title.raw: How to Train for the Belgian Waffle Ride: A Coach's Guide to America's Toughest Mixed-Surface Race
title.rendered: How to Train for the Belgian Waffle Ride: A Coach’s Guide to America’s Toughest Mixed-Surface Race

content.raw:
The Belgian Waffle Ride has grown from a California cult classic into one of the most talked-about events on the US calendar, and for good reason. It's not a road race, and it's not a gravel race — it's both, stitched together with punchy climbs, sustained dirt sectors, and a level of unpredictability that a normal century ride simply doesn't prepare you for. Depending on the location you choose (California, Utah, North Carolina, and more have joined the series), you're looking at 130-215km with anywhere from 20-40% of that on unpaved surfaces.

I've worked with riders preparing for BWR who came from a strong pure-road background, and the lesson is consistent: road fitness alone is not enough. The surface changes change everything — how you pace, how you handle the bike, and how much you need in reserve for the final unpaved sectors when the group has already split apart.

Why BWR Is a Different Physiological Problem Than a Road Century

Many riders prepare for a 200km sportive simply by riding longer every weekend. While endurance is important, A flat-out road century rewards a rider who can hold a steady, efficient effort. BWR punishes that same rider the moment the road turns to dirt, because:

  • The "waffle" itself — the course is deliberately unpredictable, mixing pavement, hardpack, sand, and rutted farm roads. Riders who've only ever trained on one surface type get caught out by the transitions, not just the terrain itself.
  • Power output becomes far more variable. Rough surfaces force constant micro-accelerations and decelerations rather than a smooth, steady wattage — this is a much higher neuromuscular and metabolic cost for the same average power.
  • Bike handling directly affects your energy expenditure. A rider who's tense and inefficient on gravel burns significantly more energy than one who's relaxed and reads the terrain well — this is trainable, but it's rarely trained.

Building the Engine: 14-18 Weeks Out

  • Mixed-surface long rides. If you have any gravel or dirt access near you, your weekly long ride should include it — even 20-30% unpaved content builds the specific handling and pacing skills BWR demands. If you're in a purely paved area, look for rail trails, fire roads, or even grass sections to simulate the surface change.
  • Variable-power interval work. Rather than smooth, steady threshold intervals, build in surges — 30 seconds hard, 30 seconds easy, repeated for 15-20 minutes — to prepare the legs for the on-off demand of technical terrain.
  • Aerobic base volume, same as any long endurance event — BWR's longer routes are firmly ultra-endurance territory, and under-cooked aerobic fitness will show up in the final third of the race regardless of how strong your gravel-specific work is.

Race-Specific Phase: 6-8 Weeks Out

  • Back-to-back long rides on tired legs, simulating the accumulated fatigue of a 6+ hour day, with the second ride including your hardest available terrain.
  • Practice riding in a group on dirt. Pack dynamics on unpaved sectors are riskier and more physically demanding than pack riding on tarmac — line choice and following distance both need to change, and that's much safer to learn in training than mid-race.
  • Dial in your equipment under race conditions, not the week before. Tire choice and pressure make a bigger difference to your result at BWR than almost any other single variable, and it needs testing on terrain that matches race day, not just around the block.

Taper: The Final Two Weeks

Drop volume, keep a small amount of intensity to stay sharp, and use this window to finalise — not experiment with — your bike setup. This is not the time to try a new tire or a new nutrition product for the first time.

Race Day: What Actually Wins or Loses You the Ride

  • Start conservatively through the first paved sections.
    It's tempting to go out hard with a fast group on smooth roads, but that effort compounds badly once the surface changes and the real work begins.
  • Fuel on a schedule, not on feel, especially through longer dirt sectors where it's harder to reach into pockets or bottles comfortably. Plan your intake around the terrain, not just the clock.
  • Relax your upper body on rough sections. Riders who grip the bars tightly and fight the terrain fatigue far faster than riders who let the bike move underneath them — this is a skill, and it's worth practicing deliberately in training, not discovering for the first time on race day.
  • Riding within your planned power or heart rate zones.
  • Eating consistently every 20–30 minutes.
  • Drinking regularly, regardless of temperature.
  • Maintaining a comfortable cadence on every climb.
  • Saving your best efforts for the final third of the route.

Many riders lose their event within the first two hours by riding above their sustainable pace.

How We Build This Into a Coaching Plan

Mixed-surface events like BWR reward a very specific blend of aerobic depth, variable-power capacity, and terrain-specific skill — and that blend looks different for every rider depending on their background and local terrain access. As part of our cycling coaching in the USA, we build plans around your actual training environment and current numbers (CP, W′, FTP), so the prep is specific to the event you're targeting rather than a generic gravel template.

FAQ

Do I need a gravel bike for the Belgian Waffle Ride, or can I ride a road bike with wider tires?
Most riders run a road bike or all-road bike with wider tires (32-38mm depending on the course) rather than a full gravel bike, since the majority of most BWR routes is still paved. Tire choice should be dictated by the specific course you're riding — check the current year's route breakdown before deciding.

How much of my training should be off-road?
As a rough guide, aim to match your training surface mix to the race's surface mix — if the course is roughly 25% unpaved, your long rides should reflect something close to that ratio in the specific-prep phase, even if your base training stays more road-focused.

Is BWR harder than a typical gravel century?
It's a different kind of hard. The surface transitions and pack dynamics on the paved sections add a tactical and technical layer that a straightforward gravel century doesn't have — most riders find the unpredictability more demanding than the raw distance or climbing.

How long before race day should I start specific preparation?
14-18 weeks gives enough time to build both the aerobic base and the surface-specific skills properly, assuming a reasonable existing fitness level. Riders starting from a lower base should allow longer.

Matteo Cigala
Founder & Head Coach
